Among efforts to study the effects of climate change on Antarctica, was aNorwegian Polar Institute project to study marine mammals. Custom-designed tags were attached to elephant seals to study the animals' habits, although researcher realized the tags could also help with field research on climate change. The electronic tags -- which fell off when the seals molted -- sent back data on temperature and salinity the oceans around Antarctica, particularly around the Fimbul Ice Shelf in east Antarctica. While ice-shelf melt has been recorded in the west of Antarctica, scientists are concerned that it could happen in the east as well. Another project to study the underside of an Antarctic glacier deployed an autonomous robot submarine. The team from the U.S. and British Antarctic Survey sent the "Autosub" on six missions to study the Pine Island Glacier and how changes in ocean temperature were affecting the West Antarctic Ice Sheet. Using sonar, the submarine picked its way around the glacier and sent back data that created three-dimensional maps that scientists used to determine where and how the warmth of the ocean waters was melting the glacier's base. "If [the West Antarctic Ice Sheet] were to melt completely, global sea levels would rise by as much as 5 meters," said Stan Jacobs, the U.S. lead scientist on the project. "Because so little is known about ice-sheet behavior, this research will take us a step further in understanding how ice sheets will contribute to sea-level rise."

(CNN) — Two of the projects conducted during the International Polar Year (IPY) used specially tagged elephant seals and sonar-equipped autonomous mini-submarines to examine how global warming is affecting the planet’s polar regions.

The fourth IPY began in March 2007, continued for two full years, and concluded last month. During that period, scientists from more than 60 nations carried out 160 research projects. Organized jointly by the International Council for Science (ICSW) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the initiative sought to improve the observation and understanding of both the Arctic and Antarctica. Approximately US$1.2 billion in international funding supported the program over its two-year duration.

In a press release, WMO Secretary-General Michel Jarraud said that the 2007/2008 International Polar Year occurred at a pivotal moment for Earth’s future. He added that new findings from polar studies would provide a stronger scientific foundation for decisions and actions taken in the years ahead.

One major discovery concerned Arctic sea ice. In the summers of 2007 and 2008, the smallest area covered by permanent, year-round ice fell to the lowest level recorded since satellite monitoring began 30 years earlier.

Research also revealed previously unrecognized effects of global warming in Antarctica, according to a report released in February by the IPY organizing committee. Further signs of climate change were documented by IPY research ships, which detected rising temperatures in the Southern Ocean. They also found that increased ice melt was producing less-salty bottom water along Antarctica’s coastline.

A Norwegian Polar Institute study of marine mammals was among the projects examining climate change’s impact on Antarctica. Researchers fitted elephant seals with purpose-built electronic tags to track their behavior. They later recognized that the devices could also gather valuable climate-related field data.

The tags transmitted information about ocean temperature and salinity in Antarctic waters, especially near the Fimbul Ice Shelf in eastern Antarctica. They detached naturally when the seals molted. Although melting ice shelves had already been documented in western Antarctica, scientists were worried that the same process might also occur in the east.

In another study, researchers used an autonomous robotic submarine to investigate the underside of an Antarctic glacier. A joint U.S. and British Antarctic Survey team sent the vessel, called “Autosub,” on six missions beneath the Pine Island Glacier. Their goal was to determine how shifts in ocean temperature were influencing the West Antarctic Ice Sheet.

Guided by sonar, Autosub navigated around the glacier and collected information used to construct three-dimensional maps. These maps helped researchers identify where and in what manner warmer seawater was eroding the glacier from below.

Stan Jacobs, the project’s lead U.S. scientist, warned that complete melting of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet could raise global sea levels by as much as five meters. Because scientists still know relatively little about how ice sheets behave, he said, the research would advance understanding of their future contribution to rising sea levels.

The 2007–2008 International Polar Year was one of the largest coordinated investigations of Earth’s polar regions ever undertaken. Researchers from more than 60 countries participated in roughly 160 scientific projects focused on the Arctic and Antarctic. By combining expertise, observations, and technology, the initiative enabled scientists to study the atmosphere, oceans, ice sheets, ecosystems, and human communities of the polar regions on a scale that would have been difficult for any nation to achieve alone.

Scientists used an unusually wide range of tools to collect information in remote and often dangerous environments. Elephant seals fitted with electronic tags gathered data on water temperature, salinity, and depth while swimming beneath Antarctic sea ice. Robotic submarines equipped with sonar mapped the underside of floating ice shelves, while satellites monitored changes in sea-ice extent and the movement of glaciers. Research vessels, aircraft, weather stations, and field teams supplied additional measurements from areas that had previously been poorly observed.

The findings showed that climate change was affecting the polar regions rapidly and extensively. During the project, Arctic summer sea ice fell to a record low, reinforcing evidence of a long-term decline in both its area and thickness. Researchers also found that waters in the Southern Ocean were warming and that this heat could reach ice shelves from below, weakening them and accelerating the flow of inland glaciers toward the sea. Observations revealed more widespread and complex melting in Antarctica than scientists had previously recognized.

Because the Arctic and Antarctic play major roles in regulating global climate and sea level, these changes have consequences far beyond the poles. The loss of reflective sea ice allows the ocean to absorb more solar energy, contributing to additional warming. Melting land ice raises global sea levels, while changes in polar oceans can influence marine ecosystems and large-scale patterns of ocean circulation.

The International Polar Year therefore provided more than a snapshot of conditions at the ends of the Earth. It strengthened international scientific cooperation, improved observing systems, and created valuable data sets for future research. Most importantly, its results offered stronger evidence that polar change was already underway, highlighting the need for governments and societies to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, prepare for unavoidable impacts, and support continued monitoring of these critical regions.

counterfactuals.output:
# Seals and robot submarines reveal a changing Antarctica

**ANTARCTICA** — Scientists taking part in the International Polar Year turned to some unconventional research partners to investigate one of the planet’s most remote regions: elephant seals and autonomous robot submarines.

The international research campaign, conducted in 2007 and 2008, brought together thousands of scientists to study the Arctic and Antarctic. Their findings helped reveal how warming oceans, melting glaciers and shifting sea ice were reshaping the polar regions — with consequences for global sea levels and climate.

Researchers fitted southern elephant seals with small electronic tags that recorded water temperature, depth and salinity as the animals dived beneath Antarctic sea ice. The instruments transmitted data by satellite whenever the seals surfaced.

Because elephant seals routinely travel hundreds of miles and dive to depths that are difficult and expensive for research vessels to reach, they collected observations from areas that had previously been almost inaccessible during winter.

The data showed how heat and ocean currents move around Antarctica, providing clues about the processes driving ice loss. The tags were designed to fall off when the seals molted, and scientists said the devices did not significantly interfere with the animals’ normal behavior.

Elsewhere, autonomous robot submarines were sent beneath floating ice shelves to map the ocean floor and measure water properties near Antarctic glaciers. Unlike ships, which can be blocked by thick ice, the unmanned vehicles could travel under ice shelves and gather information close to the point where relatively warm seawater meets glacier ice.

That boundary is crucial. Antarctic glaciers can melt from below when ocean currents carry warmer water into cavities beneath ice shelves. As the shelves thin, they lose some of their ability to hold back glaciers on land, allowing ice to flow more quickly into the sea.

Studies around rapidly changing glaciers, including Pine Island Glacier in West Antarctica, found evidence that deep ocean water was reaching beneath the ice and contributing to substantial melting.

The combination of animal-borne sensors, satellites, aircraft, ships and robotic vehicles gave researchers a more complete picture of Antarctica than traditional observations alone could provide.

Scientists say the work launched during the International Polar Year also demonstrated why long-term monitoring is essential. Conditions around Antarctica vary from year to year, but sustained measurements can help distinguish temporary fluctuations from broader climate trends.

The stakes extend far beyond the frozen continent. Antarctica contains enough ice to raise global sea levels by tens of meters if it were all to melt, though such a change would unfold over a very long period. Even a much smaller loss could increase flooding risks for coastal communities worldwide.

By recruiting deep-diving seals and deploying machines capable of navigating beneath glaciers, researchers opened new windows into one of Earth’s least understood environments — and showed that some of the most important evidence of climate change may be hidden beneath the ice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the major findings and scientific projects of the 2007–2008 International Polar Year, with details about Arctic sea ice, Antarctic warming, and sea-level risks.
counterfactuals.output:
The **2007–2008 International Polar Year (IPY)** was a coordinated research campaign led by the **International Council for Science** and the **World Meteorological Organization**. It involved tens of thousands of researchers and support personnel from more than 60 countries, organized into roughly **200–230 international projects**. Although field operations centered on March 2007–March 2009, many major findings were published afterward.

## Major scientific findings

### Arctic sea ice: rapid loss and a shift toward thinner ice

- In **September 2007**, Arctic sea ice reached a then-record-low minimum of about **4.2 million km²**, roughly **40% below the 1979–2000 average**. The 2008 minimum was only modestly larger and was the second lowest observed at that time.
- The decline was not simply a temporary reduction in area. Observations showed a major loss of **thick, multiyear ice**, increasingly replaced by thin first-year ice that melts more readily.
- The 2007 melt opened the **Northwest Passage** unusually widely and highlighted the possibility of more frequent seasonal Arctic shipping, although navigation remained hazardous and highly variable.
- IPY measurements linked sea-ice decline to warmer air and ocean temperatures, changing wind and circulation patterns, and the **ice–albedo feedback**: open water absorbs more solar energy than reflective ice, reinforcing warming.
- Arctic projects also documented thawing permafrost, changing snow cover, coastal erosion, shifts in marine ecosystems, and impacts on Indigenous communities and wildlife.

The campaign helped establish that the Arctic was not merely fluctuating around its late-20th-century state; it was moving toward a **younger, thinner, and more seasonally ice-free system**.

### Antarctic warming: strongest in West Antarctica and the Peninsula

Before IPY, Antarctic climate change was often described as a contrast between a rapidly warming Antarctic Peninsula and a relatively stable or cooling continental interior. New station records, satellite reconstruction, automatic weather stations, ice cores, and atmospheric studies produced a more complex picture:

- The **Antarctic Peninsula** remained one of the world’s fastest-warming regions during the late 20th century. Its warming contributed to the retreat and collapse of several ice shelves.
- Reconstructions published from the IPY era indicated significant warming across much of **West Antarctica**, especially around the **Amundsen Sea sector**, where major outlet glaciers drain the West Antarctic Ice Sheet.
- **East Antarctica** showed weaker and more spatially mixed trends; some areas had little warming or seasonal cooling. Thus, IPY did not show uniform warming everywhere, but it undermined the idea that warming was confined to the Peninsula.
- The partial breakup of the **Wilkins Ice Shelf in 2008**, following earlier collapses such as Larsen B in 2002, emphasized the sensitivity of ice shelves to atmospheric and oceanic warming.
- Oceanographic work showed that relatively warm **Circumpolar Deep Water** can reach the undersides of West Antarctic ice shelves, causing basal melting even where surface air temperatures remain very cold.

Later studies revised some exact estimates, but the core conclusion persisted: **West Antarctica was warming and losing ice, driven importantly by both atmospheric and ocean processes**.

### Sea-level risks: faster ice-sheet change than expected

IPY observations strengthened concern that sea level could rise faster than estimates based mainly on slow surface melting:

- Satellite gravimetry, radar and laser altimetry, GPS, and field measurements showed substantial mass loss from **Greenland** and parts of **West Antarctica**.
- Researchers observed acceleration, thinning, and retreat of outlet glaciers, particularly around Greenland and the Amundsen Sea coast of Antarctica.
- Ice shelves themselves contribute little to sea level because they already float, but they act as **buttresses** that restrain land-based glaciers. When an ice shelf thins or collapses, the glaciers behind it can accelerate and add more water to the ocean.
- IPY research therefore highlighted the importance of **dynamic ice-sheet processes**, which were not fully represented in many projections available in the 2007 IPCC assessment.
- The greatest long-term Antarctic concern was the **marine-based West Antarctic Ice Sheet**, whose bed lies largely below sea level and deepens inland in many areas. Such geometry can permit self-sustaining retreat once grounding lines become unstable.

IPY did not produce a single definitive sea-level number. Its major contribution was to show that future rise depends not only on thermal expansion and surface melting but also on potentially rapid glacier and ice-sheet dynamics. This increased concern about **multi-decadal sea-level rise** and the possibility of much larger rise over centuries if major sectors of Greenland or West Antarctica destabilize.

## Important IPY projects and programs

- **DAMOCLES** – Integrated observations and modeling of Arctic sea ice, ocean circulation, atmosphere, and climate feedbacks.
- **SEARCH and related Arctic observing efforts** – Investigated long-term environmental change across the Arctic.
- **International Arctic Buoy Programme and ocean mooring networks** – Expanded real-time measurements of ice drift, ocean heat, salinity, and atmospheric conditions.
- **Arctic and Antarctic marine biodiversity censuses** – Catalogued polar marine life, discovering previously unknown organisms and documenting ecosystem responses to ice and temperature change.
- **AGAP—Antarctica’s Gamburtsev Province Project** – Used aircraft carrying radar, gravity, and magnetic instruments to map the buried **Gamburtsev Subglacial Mountains** beneath East Antarctica and study the origins of the Antarctic ice sheet.
- **POLENET** – Deployed GPS and seismic stations to measure crustal motion, ice-mass changes, and Earth structure beneath Greenland and Antarctica.
- **ANDRILL** – Drilled sediment cores beneath and near the Ross Ice Shelf, revealing that Antarctic ice and ice shelves had retreated substantially during earlier warm periods, demonstrating long-term sensitivity to climate change.
- **ITASE and ice-core programs** – Reconstructed past snowfall, atmospheric circulation, temperature, volcanic events, and pollution.
- **Ice-sheet traverse and airborne radar surveys** – Mapped ice thickness, bedrock topography, subglacial lakes, and potential pathways of ice-sheet retreat.
- **Permafrost and terrestrial ecosystem networks** – Measured ground warming, carbon storage, hydrology, vegetation change, and infrastructure risks.
- **Human-dimensions and Indigenous knowledge projects** – Examined health, food security, community adaptation, transportation, and the value of local observations in understanding Arctic change.

## Overall significance

The IPY transformed polar science from a collection of national programs into a more integrated **international observing system**. Its broad message was that the polar regions were changing faster and in more interconnected ways than previously recognized:

1. Arctic summer sea ice was shrinking and becoming structurally more vulnerable.
2. Antarctic warming and ice loss extended beyond the Peninsula, especially into West Antarctica.
3. Ocean-driven melting and glacier acceleration created sea-level risks that simple surface-melt models could miss.
4. Polar change had global consequences for climate feedbacks, ecosystems, ocean circulation, and coastal societies.

Many IPY observing networks, data archives, and international partnerships continued afterward, forming part of the foundation for today’s assessments of Arctic amplification, Antarctic ice-sheet instability, and global sea-level rise.

counterfactuals.output:
## Elephant seals and robot submarine help scientists probe Antarctica’s hidden waters

**ANTARCTICA —** Researchers are combining an unusual team of animal assistants and robotic technology to gather climate data from some of the Southern Ocean’s least accessible waters.

Scientists fitted elephant seals with small satellite-linked instruments that measured water temperature, salinity and depth as the animals dived beneath Antarctic sea ice. The tags transmitted summaries of the measurements whenever the seals surfaced, providing observations from winter months and ice-covered areas that research ships often cannot reach.

Elephant seals are particularly useful for this work because they routinely dive hundreds of metres and travel thousands of kilometres while searching for food. Their movements allow researchers to build a broad picture of how heat and salt are distributed around Antarctica. The tags are designed to fall off after the seals moult.

The autonomous submarine **Autosub** provided a complementary view. Programmed to navigate without a crew or a cable to the surface, the vehicle travelled beneath ice and collected high-resolution measurements along planned routes. Its sensors recorded properties such as temperature, salinity, water movement and the shape of the ice above or seabed below, depending on the mission.

Together, the two methods address different gaps in Antarctic monitoring. The seals cover wide areas over long periods, although scientists cannot control exactly where they swim. Autosub can follow a precise survey path and carry more sophisticated equipment, but its missions are shorter and require careful launch and recovery.

The resulting data help scientists track currents carrying relatively warm ocean water toward ice shelves. That heat can melt floating ice from below, thinning the shelves that slow the movement of glaciers into the sea. Researchers can also use the observations to improve climate and sea-level models and to study the formation of cold, dense water that helps drive global ocean circulation.

By combining biologging with autonomous vehicles, researchers are obtaining year-round evidence from an environment where conventional ship-based observations remain difficult, dangerous and expensive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the International Polar Year’s scope, funding, participating countries, key global-warming findings, and innovative polar research methods in an article suitable for a general audience.
counterfactuals.output:
# International Polar Year: A Planetwide Effort to Understand a Rapidly Changing Arctic and Antarctic

From March 2007 to March 2009, scientists mounted the largest coordinated investigation of Earth’s polar regions in half a century. Known as the **International Polar Year, or IPY**, the campaign examined not only ice and climate, but also oceans, wildlife, geology, atmospheric chemistry, human communities and the connections between the poles and the rest of the planet.

Although called a “year,” the program lasted two full years so researchers could observe complete seasonal cycles in both the Arctic and Antarctic.

## Global scope and funding

The IPY was organized principally by the **International Council for Science**, now the International Science Council, and the **World Meteorological Organization**. It encompassed more than 200 international projects and involved tens of thousands of scientists, technicians, teachers, students and community participants.

There was no single central IPY budget. National governments, research agencies and institutions financed their own projects and infrastructure. Estimates commonly place total worldwide spending at **about US$1.2 billion**, although the figure varies depending on whether ships, aircraft, satellites, stations and existing national programs are counted.

More than 60 countries participated—often reported as roughly **63 nations**. They included established polar-research powers such as the United States, Canada, Russia, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Greenland, Iceland, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, China, India, South Korea, South Africa, Argentina, Chile and Brazil. Scientists from countries without polar territory also joined, making IPY a genuinely international undertaking. Arctic Indigenous communities contributed observations, expertise and local knowledge as well.

## What scientists learned about global warming

IPY took place during a period of unusually dramatic polar change. Its observations strengthened evidence that warming was occurring especially rapidly in the Arctic and was affecting both polar regions in interconnected ways.

Among the major findings were:

- **Arctic sea ice was shrinking and thinning.** In September 2007, Arctic sea-ice extent fell to what was then the lowest level recorded by satellite. IPY research showed that the ice cover was losing older, thicker multiyear ice and becoming increasingly dominated by thinner seasonal ice.
- **The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets were losing mass.** Satellite and aircraft measurements revealed substantial ice loss, particularly along Greenland’s margins and in West Antarctica. Faster-flowing outlet glaciers demonstrated that ice sheets can respond more quickly to warming oceans and air than scientists had once assumed.
- **Ocean warming was attacking ice from below.** Researchers found that relatively warm ocean water was reaching glaciers and floating ice shelves, accelerating melting and contributing to glacier retreat.
- **Permafrost was warming.** Measurements across the Arctic showed rising ground temperatures and deeper seasonal thaw. This threatened roads, buildings and pipelines and raised concern that thawing soils could release additional carbon dioxide and methane.
- **Polar ecosystems were shifting.** Changes in sea ice, snow cover and ocean conditions affected plankton, fish, seabirds and marine mammals. On land, shrubs were expanding into some tundra areas, while animals and plants faced altered habitats and seasonal timing.
- **Polar change had global consequences.** Melting land ice contributed to sea-level rise, while changes in snow and sea ice reduced the amount of sunlight reflected back into space. This darker surface absorbed more heat, reinforcing warming through the “ice-albedo feedback.”

The findings did not mean that every part of the poles warmed at the same rate. East Antarctica, for example, behaved differently from the Antarctic Peninsula and West Antarctica. IPY’s broad measurements helped scientists understand this regional complexity while confirming the overall vulnerability of polar systems.

## New ways of exploring the poles

IPY was notable not just for its scale but also for how researchers worked. It combined traditional field expeditions with technologies capable of observing vast, inaccessible areas year-round.

**Satellites** measured sea-ice extent, ice-sheet elevation, glacier motion and changes in gravity caused by lost ice mass. **Aircraft equipped with radar and laser instruments** mapped the thickness of ice sheets and revealed buried mountain ranges, lakes and landscapes beneath the ice.

In the oceans, scientists deployed **autonomous underwater vehicles, instrumented floats, drifting buoys and ice-tethered profilers**. These devices collected data beneath sea ice and through the polar winter, when ships could not operate. Some marine mammals were fitted with harmless electronic tags that recorded temperature, depth and salinity while the animals moved through otherwise poorly sampled waters.

Researchers also expanded networks of **automatic weather stations, seismometers, GPS receivers and permafrost boreholes**. New observatories linked measurements of the atmosphere, ocean, ice and living organisms rather than studying each in isolation.

Equally important was the growing use of **community-based monitoring and Indigenous knowledge**. Arctic residents contributed detailed understanding of sea ice, weather, wildlife and travel conditions developed through generations of experience. Social scientists studied how environmental change affected food security, infrastructure, health and culture.

## A lasting legacy

The International Polar Year produced large shared datasets, new research stations and observing networks, improved climate and ice-sheet models, and a generation of scientists trained in international collaboration. It also showed that the Arctic and Antarctic are not remote, self-contained worlds. Changes at the poles influence sea level, ocean circulation, ecosystems and climate far beyond the regions where they begin.

Its central message was clear: the poles are changing rapidly, and understanding those changes requires sustained observations, cooperation across national borders and the combined insights of technology, field science and the people who live in polar environments.

counterfactuals.output:
# Climate Change at the Poles: Evidence from the Arctic and Antarctic

The Arctic and Antarctic are among the clearest indicators of a warming planet. Although the two polar regions differ greatly—the Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, while Antarctica is a continent surrounded by ocean—both are undergoing significant changes in sea ice, glaciers, ice shelves, and ocean temperatures.

## Record-low summer sea ice

One of the most visible signs of climate change is the decline of Arctic summer sea ice. Satellite measurements show that both the extent and thickness of Arctic ice have fallen substantially since observations began in 1979. In September 2012, Arctic sea ice reached the lowest summer extent in the satellite record at the time. Recent years have consistently remained well below the late-20th-century average, indicating a long-term decline rather than an isolated event.

The loss of bright, reflective ice also creates a feedback loop. Open ocean absorbs more solar energy than ice, causing additional warming and making future ice loss more likely. Declining sea ice affects Arctic ecosystems and communities, while potentially influencing weather patterns farther south.

Antarctic sea ice behaves differently and varies more strongly from year to year. After several decades without the same clear downward trend seen in the Arctic, Antarctic sea ice fell to exceptionally low levels in recent years, setting record-low seasonal extents in satellite observations. Scientists are investigating how warming oceans, shifting winds, and natural variability have combined to produce these changes.

## Warming waters in the Southern Ocean

Much of the heat added to Earth’s climate system is absorbed by the oceans. The Southern Ocean surrounding Antarctica has taken up a particularly large share of this excess heat. Warmer water can circulate beneath floating ice shelves, melting them from below even when surface air temperatures remain below freezing.

This process is especially important because ice shelves act as barriers that slow the movement of land-based glaciers into the sea. Their melting does not directly raise sea level by much because they already float, but their thinning or collapse can allow inland ice to flow faster, increasing sea-level rise.

## The Fimbul Ice Shelf

The Fimbul Ice Shelf in East Antarctica illustrates the complexity of interactions between ocean water and Antarctic ice. Scientists have studied whether relatively warm deep water can reach the cavity beneath the shelf and increase basal melting. Research suggests that local ocean circulation, winds, sea ice, and the shape of the seafloor influence how much heat reaches the ice.

Fimbul has generally not experienced the extreme melting observed beneath some West Antarctic ice shelves. Nevertheless, it remains an important monitoring site because changes in Southern Ocean circulation could alter the delivery of warm water to its underside. Observations there also help scientists improve models of how Antarctic ice shelves may respond to future warming.

## Pine Island Glacier

Pine Island Glacier in West Antarctica is one of the continent’s fastest-changing glaciers. It drains a large portion of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet into the Amundsen Sea. Warm ocean water has penetrated beneath its floating ice shelf, causing substantial thinning and retreat.

As the ice shelf weakens, it provides less resistance to the glacier behind it. Pine Island Glacier can then accelerate, carrying more land ice into the ocean. The glacier is particularly vulnerable because much of its bed lies below sea level and slopes downward toward the interior. Once retreat begins along such terrain, it may become difficult to stop—a process known as marine ice-sheet instability.

## The risk from the West Antarctic Ice Sheet

The wider West Antarctic Ice Sheet is a major concern for future sea levels. If it were to melt completely, it contains enough ice to raise global mean sea level by roughly five meters. Such a loss would not occur all at once and would likely unfold over centuries or longer, but some studies suggest that parts of the ice sheet may already be committed to prolonged retreat.

A five-meter rise would radically reshape coastlines, inundate many low-lying cities and islands, increase storm-surge risks, and force large-scale adaptation or migration. The exact rate and extent of future ice loss remain uncertain because they depend on greenhouse-gas emissions, ocean circulation, snowfall, ice-sheet dynamics, and the stability of remaining ice shelves.

## A global warning

Changes in polar ice are not remote events with only local consequences. Arctic sea-ice loss alters ecosystems and the planet’s energy balance, while Antarctic glacier retreat adds water to the global ocean. Evidence from record-low summer sea ice, warming Southern Ocean waters, the Fimbul Ice Shelf, and the rapid retreat of Pine Island Glacier shows that the poles are responding to a changing climate.

Continued satellite monitoring, ocean measurements, field research, and improved computer modeling are essential for determining how quickly these changes will unfold. Reducing greenhouse-gas emissions remains the most important way to limit long-term warming and lower the risk of severe, irreversible ice loss.
